DEPARTMENT 730 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 21STV37592    Hearing Date: July 2, 2026    Dept: 730

TENTATIVE 

 

The request for default judgment submitted on March 27, 2026 is DENIED for the following reasons: 

 

  • Plaintiff has not dismissed DOE defendants or Defendant Philip A. Madsen, nor has Plaintiff applied for separate relief as to these other defendants. (CRC 3.1800(a)(7).) 

  • Plaintiff’s declaration fails to support the amount of damages requested.  Plaintiff’s testimony does not address the amount of damages.  Plaintiff attaches certain medical records as Exhibits A, B and C but the exhibits are unauthenticated.  In addition, Plaintiff’s Exhibit A contains a document entitled “Transaction Type Summary” that reflects charges of $68,536 for services provided between 10/9/19 and 10/15/25.  Plaintiff is requesting special damages in the amount of $69,036, which is more than reflected in the “Transaction Type Summary.”  Plaintiff’s request for special damages is not supported by the evidence. 

  • Plaintiff’s general damages are also unsupported by the evidence. Plaintiff is asking $345,180 in general damages, which is five times her requested special damages.  Based on her declaration testimony regarding what occurred and the medical records, the amount of general damages is excessive.   

 

No later than September 1, 2026, Plaintiff is to submit a new default judgment package correcting these defects. Failure to do so may result in the imposition of sanctions, including monetary sanctions and/or dismissal. The OSC re entry of default judgment is continued to September 29, 2026. 

Case Number: 25STCV11271    Hearing Date: July 2, 2026    Dept: 730

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles 

Department 730 

¿ 

 

SAMANTHA MURPHY, an individual doing business as SWB Entertainment, 

vs. 

JOSHUA JOHNSON, et al., 

Defendant(s). 

Case No.: 

25STCV11271 

Hearing Date: 

July 6, 2026 

 

 

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: PLAINTIFF’S MOTION TO LIFT STAY OF PROCEEDINGS 

 

I. BACKGROUND 

On April 17, 2025, Plaintiff Samantha Murphy (“Plaintiff”) filed her complaint against Defendants Joshua Johnson, Amanda Conrad, Dixon Talent, Inc., and Does 1 through 20, inclusive (“Defendants”). Plaintiff alleges nine causes of action against Defendants for (1) Breach of Contract; (2) Breach of Implied Covenant of Good Faith and Fair Dealing; (3) Unjust Enrichment; (4) Constructive Fraud; (5) Negligent Hiring, Supervision, and Retention; (6) Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress; (7) Defamation Per Se (Libel); (8) Violation of California Penal Code § 502 (Unauthorized Access & Data Misuse); and (9) Civil Conspiracy/Aiding and Abetting. Plaintiff alleges Defendants unlawfully removed Plaintiff from her long-standing position as professional representative and business partner to Defendant Joshua Johnson. Plaintiff alleges that she is a licensed and bonded talent agent who primarily serves as an independent artist representative under the business SWB Entertainment.   

On November 20, 2025, the Court granted the Motion for Stay of Proceedings pending determination of controversy by Labor Commissioner of issues arising under the Talent Agencies Act (“TAA”).  

On May 18, 2026, Plaintiff submitted a Status Conference Statement requesting that the Court lift the stay of this action.  

On May 27, 2026, Plaintiff filed this Motion to Lift Stay of Proceedings (“Motion”) as to all causes of action, or alternatively, to all causes of action the Labor Commissioner has no jurisdiction. Defendants opposed Plaintiff’s Motion. Plaintiff did not file a reply.  

 

II. LEGAL STANDARD 

The purpose of the TAA is “remedial; its purpose is to protect artists seeking professional employment from the abuses of talent agencies.” (Styne v. Stevens (2001) 26 Cal.4th 42, 50.) Under the TAA, “no person shall engage in or carry on the occupation of a talent agency without first procuring a license therefor from the Labor Commissioner.” (Lab. Code, § 1700.5.) A “talent agency” means “a person or corporation who engages in the occupation of procuring, offering, promising, or attempting to procure employment or engagements for an artist…”¿ (Lab. Code, § 1700.4, subd. (a).) 

When the Talent Agencies Act (“TAA”) is invoked in the course of a contract dispute, the Commissioner has exclusive jurisdiction to determine his jurisdiction over the matter, including whether the contract involved the services of a talent agency. (Styne, supra, 26 Cal.4th at 54.) A claim to this effect must first be submitted to the Commissioner, and that forum must be exhausted, before the matter can be determined by the superior court. (Id. at pp. 55-56.) Thus, disputes must be heard by the Commissioner, and all remedies before the Commissioner must be exhausted before the parties can proceed to the superior court. (Blanks v. Seyfarth Shaw LLP (2009) 171 Cal.App.4th 336, 365.) The TAA statutory scheme creates an absolute bar to plaintiffs who wish to circumvent the pre-suit requirement of filing first with the Commissioner. (Ibid.) After the issues are first addressed by the Commissioner, both parties have the right to a trial de novo. (Id. at p. 360.) 

 

III. DISCUSSION 

Plaintiff contends that the continued stay of this action is no longer warranted and causes ongoing prejudice to Plaintiff’s due process rights and right to timely resolve her claims. Plaintiff claims that eight months have passed since the filing of the petition with the Labor Commissioner to resolve the licensing controversy and, since then, no hearing has been set. Furthermore, Plaintiff argues that the Court is the ultimate forum for licensing questions and that the petition lacks merit. Additionally, Defendants have failed to prosecute the administrative proceeding with reasonable diligence.  

In opposition, Defendants argue that the alleged licensing issue is an issue reserved for the Labor Commissioner. Defendants also argue that the Court lacks jurisdiction over this dispute until the Labor Commissioner has acted. Moreover, the timeline is routine and outside Defendant’s control. The passage of time does not constitute a basis for reconsideration of the stay. Finally, a partial lift would create piecemeal litigation over claims arising from the same contractual relationship and has no support in statute or case law.  

The Court previously granted Defendant’s Motion for Stay of Proceedings pending determination of controversy by Labor Commissioner of issues arising under the TAA. The Court agrees with Defendants that the Labor Commissioner must first decide those issues before the dispute may be considered by the court. (Blanks, supra, 171 Cal.App.4th at 365.) Here, the Labor Commissioner has not yet set a hearing or reviewed Defendants’ petition. Thus, the administrative remedy has not been exhausted, and the dispute may not proceed to the superior court.  

The Court does not find persuasive Plaintiff’s argument that Plaintiff is prejudiced by the time the Labor Commission will take to review this Petition. The Labor Commissioner has advised that it may take months for the hearing to be scheduled. (George Decl., ¶ 5.) This scheduling is not within Defendants’ control. Plaintiff has provided no evidence of prejudice beyond stating conclusively that Plaintiff has been “suspended in procedural limbo” and that the delay may be resolved by the Court’s own de novo review the issues. Thus, the Court does not find that Plaintiff has been prejudiced by the Labor Commissioner’s timeline. 

Moreover, Plaintiff’s argument that the issues may be reviewed de novo is misplaced. The parties have a right to a trial de novo only after Labor Commissioner has first considered the issues. As the petition has not yet been reviewed by the Labor Commissioner, the Court would usurp the purpose of TAA by lifting the stay of the proceedings and denying the Labor Commission review. (See Styne, supra, 26 Cal.4th at p. 54 [“The Talent Agencies Act specifies that “[i]n cases of controversy arising under this chapter, the parties involved shall refer the matters in dispute to the Labor Commissioner, who shall hear and determine the same, subject to an appeal ... to the superior court where the same shall be heard de novo.”]) 

Accordingly, the Motion is denied. 

 

IV. CONCLUSION 

Plaintiff’s Motion to Lift Stay of Proceedings is DENIED. 

 

Moving Party is ordered to give notice. 

 

DATED: July 6, 2026 

__________________________ 

Hon. Alexander C.D. Giza 

Judge of the Superior Court

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles 

Department 730 

¿ 

NORMAN KAI LEE, 

Plaintiff, 

vs. 

DEMETRIUS TENNELL LOCKETT, TOWNSEND & LOCKETT, DEITRA CRAWLEY, JANET SCOTT, SHANI WHISONANT, DOES 1 THROUGH 10, INCLUSIVE, et al., 

Defendants. 

Case No.: 

25STCV15616 

Hearing Date: 

July 2, 2026 

 

 

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: DEFENDANT DEMETRIUS TENNELL LOCKETT’S MOTION TO VACATE ENTRY OF DEFAULT 

 

I. BACKGROUND 

On May 29, 2025, Plaintiff Norman Kai Lee (“Plaintiff”) filed a complaint against Defendants Demetrius Tennell Lockett (“Lockett”), Townsend & Lockett (“T&L”), Deitra Crawley (“Crawley”), Janet Scott (“Scott”), Shani Whisonant (“Whisonant”), and Does 1 through 10 (collectively, “Defendants”), alleging causes of action for (1) unauthorized practice of law, (2) tortious interference with contract, (3) civil extortion, (4) violation of Business & Professions Code §17200, (5) abuse of process, (6) negligent misrepresentation, and (7) intentional infliction of emotional distress. Plaintiff alleges Defendants operated with a suspended business license and were not licensed to practice law in California but did so and coerced and intimidated Plaintiff through their unauthorized practice of law. 

On October 21, 2025, the Court entered default against Scott. 

On December 1, 2025, the Court entered default against Lockett, T&L, Crawley, and Whisonant.  

On March 4, 2026, Lockett filed the instant motion to vacate entry of default. 

On June 24, 2026, Lockett filed a reply. 

As of June 26, 2026, Plaintiff has not filed an opposition. 

 

II. LEGAL STANDARD 

Code of Civil Procedure (“CCP”)¿§ 473(b) states:¿“The court may, upon any terms as may be just, relieve a party or his or her legal representative from a judgment, dismissal, order, or other proceeding taken against him or her through his or her mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect. Application for this relief … shall be made within a reasonable time, in no case exceeding six months, after the judgment, dismissal, order, or proceeding was taken. … Notwithstanding any other requirements of this section, the court shall, whenever an application for relief is made no more than six months after entry of judgment, is in proper form, and is accompanied by an attorney's sworn affidavit attesting to his or her mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect, vacate any … dismissal entered against his or her client, unless the court¿finds that the default or dismissal was not in fact caused by the attorney's mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect. The court shall, whenever relief is granted based on an attorney's¿affidavit¿of fault, direct the attorney to pay reasonable compensatory legal fees and costs to opposing counsel or parties.”¿ 

“When service of a summons has not resulted in actual notice to a party in time to defend the action and a default or default judgment has been entered against the party in the action, the party may serve and file a notice of motion to set aside the default or default judgment and for leave to defend the action. The notice of motion shall be served and filed within a reasonable time, but in no event exceeding the earlier of: (i)¿two years after entry of a default judgment against the party; or (ii)¿180 days after service on the party of a written notice that the default or default judgment has been entered.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 473.5, subd. (a).)  

 

III. DISCUSSION 

Lockett moves to vacate the entry of default against him pursuant to CCP § 473 on the grounds of mistake, inadvertence, and/or excusable neglect and pursuant to CCP § 473.5 on the grounds that Plaintiff’s defective pleading requires that default be set aside. 

Lockett is the managing partner of T&L. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 2.) Lockett acknowledges that Plaintiff’s service agent purports to have diligently sought to personally serve Defendants at T&L’s Atlanta offices but states he never received any communication regarding service on Defendants. (Lockett Decl., ¶¶ 5-6.) Lockett learned of Plaintiff’s purported service efforts by reviewing the docket in this action. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 6.) Lockett’s contact information is on T&L’s website, and Plaintiff sent Lockett one or more emails prior to bringing this lawsuit, but Lockett was never contacted regarding service of process. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 6.) 

On June 6, 2025, Lockett received copies of the summons and complaint, but all summonses were directed to all defendants in an “omnibus fashion.” (Lockett Decl., ¶ 7.) Further, the complaint, its verification, and certificate of service were unsigned. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 7; Exhs. A-B.) Lockett understood that the attempted service was not perfected until a mailed copy was sent by U.S. mail. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 8.) Therefore, he chose to watch for a U.S. mail delivery of the summons and complaint, which he never received. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 8.) 

Then, on July 12, 2025, Lockett received a copy of Plaintiff’s request for entry of default, but because he had not received a mailed copy of the summons and complaint, he emailed Plaintiff to inform him that service was unperfected and defective. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 9; Exh. C.) Lockett and T&L never received copies of the summons and complaint in this action. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 10.) However, near the end of 2025, Lockett learned of Plaintiff’s efforts to secure default against Defendants, so Lockett began reviewing the docket for this action. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 11.) On December 30, 2025, Lockett sent Plaintiff another email advising him that service remained unperfected and offered to discuss a stipulation to accept service, which Plaintiff did not accept. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 11; Exh. D.)  

Lockett argues default must be set aside because Plaintiff’s pleadings are defective, as Plaintiff filed an unexecuted version of the complaint and attempted service with the same unexecuted version, rendering service defective. Lockett further argues he is entitled to have default set aside for excusable neglect or inadvertence because he never received a mailed copy of the summons and complaint, and it was excusable neglect for Lockett to have not filed a response to the complaint earlier despite his knowledge of the complaint.     

The Court finds that Lockett sufficiently establishes that default be set aside. “If the court has acquired jurisdiction, i.e., summons has been served, but service of summons has not resulted in actual notice to a defendant, although the defendant has acquired actual knowledge of the action from another source, this does not preclude a defendant from seeking relief under section 473.5.” (Olvera v. Olvera (1991) 232 Cal.App.3d 32, 40.) The Court of Appeal found that “section 473.5 reflects the understanding that if any form of service of summons does not result in actual knowledge, fundamental fairness may require that a subsequent default be set aside.” (Ibid.) “Until summons is served, there is no need to respond . . . .” (Ibid.) Here, Lockett acquired actual notice of the summon and complaint because he received copies. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 7.) Further, Lockett learned of Plaintiff’s efforts to secure default against Defendants near the end of 2025. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 11.) Therefore, Lockett had actual notice.  

However, the Court agrees with Lockett that Plaintiff’s pleading was defective. “Every pleading, petition, written notice of motion, or other similar paper shall be signed by at least one attorney of record in the attorney’s individual name, or, if the party is not represented by an attorney, shall be signed by the party. Each paper shall state the signer’s address and telephone number, if any. Except when otherwise provided by law, pleadings need not be verified or accompanied by affidavit. An unsigned paper shall be stricken unless omission of the signature is corrected promptly after being called to the attention of the attorney or party.” (Code Civ. Proc., 128.7, subd. (a).) Plaintiff’s complaint was unsigned. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 7; Exhs. A-B.) Lockett brought to Plaintiff’s attention that service was unperfected and defective, which Plaintiff did not correct. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 9; Exh. C.) Therefore, pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 128.7, subdivision (a), the unsigned papers shall be stricken.  

Additionally, Plaintiff does not oppose this motion, demonstrating correction of the unperfected and defective service. Thus, Lockett is entitled to have the default set aside. 

 

IV. CONCLUSION 

Defendant Lockett’s motion to vacate entry of default is GRANTED. 

 

Moving Party is ordered to give notice. 

 

DATED: July 2, 2026 

__________________________ 

Hon. Alexander C.D. Giza 

Judge of the Superior Court

July 2, 2026 

 

 

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: DEFENDANT JANET SCOTT’S MOTION TO VACATE ENTRY OF DEFAULT 

 

I. BACKGROUND 

On May 29, 2025, Plaintiff Norman Kai Lee (“Plaintiff”) filed a complaint against Defendants Demetrius Tennell Lockett (“Lockett”), Townsend & Lockett (“T&L”), Deitra Crawley (“Crawley”), Janet Scott (“Scott”), Shani Whisonant (“Whisonant”), and Does 1 through 10 (collectively, “Defendants”), alleging causes of action for (1) unauthorized practice of law, (2) tortious interference with contract, (3) civil extortion, (4) violation of Business & Professions Code §17200, (5) abuse of process, (6) negligent misrepresentation, and (7) intentional infliction of emotional distress. Plaintiff alleges Defendants operated with a suspended business license and were not licensed to practice law in California but did so and coerced and intimidated Plaintiff through their unauthorized practice of law. 

On October 21, 2025, the Court entered default against Scott. 

On December 1, 2025, the Court entered default against Lockett, T&L, Crawley, and Whisonant.  

On March 4, 2026, Scott filed the instant motion to vacate entry of default. 

On June 23, 2026, Scott filed a reply. 

As of June 25, 2026, Plaintiff has not filed an opposition. 

 

II. LEGAL STANDARD 

Code of Civil Procedure (“CCP”)¿§ 473(b) states:¿“The court may, upon any terms as may be just, relieve a party or his or her legal representative from a judgment, dismissal, order, or other proceeding taken against him or her through his or her mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect. Application for this relief … shall be made within a reasonable time, in no case exceeding six months, after the judgment, dismissal, order, or proceeding was taken. … Notwithstanding any other requirements of this section, the court shall, whenever an application for relief is made no more than six months after entry of judgment, is in proper form, and is accompanied by an attorney's sworn affidavit attesting to his or her mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect, vacate any … dismissal entered against his or her client, unless the court¿finds that the default or dismissal was not in fact caused by the attorney's mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect. The court shall, whenever relief is granted based on an attorney's¿affidavit¿of fault, direct the attorney to pay reasonable compensatory legal fees and costs to opposing counsel or parties.”¿ 

“When service of a summons has not resulted in actual notice to a party in time to defend the action and a default or default judgment has been entered against the party in the action, the party may serve and file a notice of motion to set aside the default or default judgment and for leave to defend the action. The notice of motion shall be served and filed within a reasonable time, but in no event exceeding the earlier of: (i)¿two years after entry of a default judgment against the party; or (ii)¿180 days after service on the party of a written notice that the default or default judgment has been entered.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 473.5, subd. (a).)  

 

III. DISCUSSION 

Scott moves to vacate the entry of default against her pursuant to CCP § 473 on the grounds of mistake, inadvertence, and/or excusable neglect and pursuant to CCP § 473.5 on the grounds that Plaintiff’s defective pleading requires that default be set aside. 

Scott previously worked at T&L as a corporate attorney but left her employment there on June 2, 2025. (Scott Decl., ¶ 2; Lockett Decl., ¶ 2.) Scott never received a copy of the summons and complaint, notice from Plaintiff that he initiated an action, or a copy of any filing in the action. (Scott Decl., ¶ 4.) Lockett, the managing partner for T&L, acknowledges that Plaintiff’s service agent purports to have diligently sought to personally serve Defendants at T&L’s Atlanta offices, but states he never received any communication regarding service on Defendants. (Lockett Decl., ¶¶ 5-6.) Lockett learned of Plaintiff’s purported service efforts by reviewing the docket in this action. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 6.) Lockett’s contact information is on T&L’s website, and Plaintiff sent Lockett one or more emails prior to bringing this lawsuit, but Lockett was never contacted regarding service of process. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 6.) 

On June 6, 2025, Lockett received copies of the summons and complaint, but all summonses were directed to all defendants in an “omnibus fashion.” (Lockett Decl., ¶ 7.) Further, the complaint, its verification, and certificate of service were unsigned. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 7; Exhs. A-B.) Lockett did not provide copies to the named defendants because they no longer worked at T&L and he understood that the attempted service was not perfected until a mailed copy was sent by U.S. mail. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 8.) Therefore, he chose to watch for a U.S. mail delivery of the summons and complaint, which he never received. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 8.) 

Then, on July 12, 2025, Lockett received a copy of Plaintiff’s request for entry of default, but because he had not received a mailed copy of the summons and complaint, he emailed Plaintiff to inform him that service was unperfected and defective. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 9; Exh. C.) Lockett and T&L never received copies of the summons and complaint in this action. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 10.) However, near the end of 2025, Lockett learned of Plaintiff’s efforts to secure default against Defendants, so Lockett began reviewing the docket for this action. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 11.) On December 30, 2025, Lockett sent Plaintiff another email advising him that service remained unperfected and offered to discuss a stipulation to accept service, which Plaintiff did not accept. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 11; Exh. D.)  

Scott became aware of this lawsuit on January 4, 2026 when contacted by Lockett, her former manager partner, about Plaintiff’s lawsuit. (Scott Decl., ¶ 5; Lockett Decl., ¶ 12.) Scott was unaware of Plaintiff’s efforts to obtain default judgment against her and, after she learned of the lawsuit, quickly engaged counsel to represent her. (Scott Decl., ¶ 5.) Scott argues she lacked actual notice of this lawsuit in time to properly respond and Plaintiff’s efforts to serve her were wholly deficient. Scott further argues she is entitled to have default set aside for excusable neglect or inadvertence because Plaintiff delivered the complaint to her former employer, without a pre-suit investigation to her whereabouts of employment at the time of suit or service.  

The Court finds that Scott sufficiently attests that Lockett’s mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect caused the default against Scott. Further, the Court finds that Scott sufficiently establishes that Plaintiff’s defective pleading requires that default be set aside under CCP § 473.5(a). Notably, Plaintiff does not oppose this motion. 

 

IV. CONCLUSION 

Defendant Scott’s motion to vacate entry of default is GRANTED. 

 

Moving Party is ordered to give notice.

On June 6, 2025, Lockett received copies of the summons and complaint, but all summonses were directed to all defendants in an “omnibus fashion.” (Lockett Decl., ¶ 7.) Further, the complaint, its verification, and certificate of service were unsigned. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 7; Exhs. A-B.) Lockett did not provide copies to the named defendants because they no longer worked at T&L and he understood that the attempted service was not perfected until a mailed copy was sent by U.S. mail. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 8.) Therefore, he chose to watch for a U.S. mail delivery of the summons and complaint, which he never received. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 8.) 

Then, on July 12, 2025, Lockett received a copy of Plaintiff’s request for entry of default, but because he had not received a mailed copy of the summons and complaint, he emailed Plaintiff to inform him that service was unperfected and defective. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 9; Exh. C.) Lockett and T&L never received copies of the summons and complaint in this action. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 10.) However, near the end of 2025, Lockett learned of Plaintiff’s efforts to secure default against Defendants, so Lockett began reviewing the docket for this action. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 11.) On December 30, 2025, Lockett sent Plaintiff another email advising him that service remained unperfected and offered to discuss a stipulation to accept service, which Plaintiff did not accept. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 11; Exh. D.)  

Whisonant became aware of this lawsuit on January 4, 2026 when contacted by Lockett, her former manager partner, about Plaintiff’s lawsuit. (Whisonant Decl., ¶ 5; Lockett Decl., ¶ 12.) Whisonant was unaware of Plaintiff’s efforts to obtain default judgment against her and, after she learned of the lawsuit, quickly engaged counsel to represent her. (Whisonant Decl., ¶ 5.) Whisonant argues she lacked actual notice of this lawsuit in time to properly respond and Plaintiff’s efforts to serve her were wholly deficient. Whisonant further argues she is entitled to have default set aside for excusable neglect or inadvertence because Plaintiff delivered the complaint to her former employer, without a pre-suit investigation into her whereabouts or employment at the time of suit or service.  

The Court finds that Whisonant sufficiently establishes that default should be set aside. “If the court has acquired jurisdiction, i.e., summons has been served, but service of summons has not resulted in actual notice to a defendant, although the defendant has acquired actual knowledge of the action from another source, this does not preclude a defendant from seeking relief under section 473.5.” (Olvera v. Olvera (1991) 232 Cal.App.3d 32, 40.) The Court of Appeal found that “section 473.5 reflects the understanding that if any form of service of summons does not result in actual knowledge, fundamental fairness may require that a subsequent default be set aside.” (Ibid.) “Until summons is served, there is no need to respond . . . .” (Ibid.) Here, Whisonant lacked actual notice of the summons and complaint because she never received a copy of the summons and complaint, nor did Plaintiff alert her that he had initiated the action. (Whisonant Decl., ¶ 4.)  

Further, the Court agrees with Whisonant that Plaintiff’s pleading was defective. “Every pleading, petition, written notice of motion, or other similar paper shall be signed by at least one attorney of record in the attorney’s individual name, or, if the party is not represented by an attorney, shall be signed by the party. Each paper shall state the signer’s address and telephone number, if any. Except when otherwise provided by law, pleadings need not be verified or accompanied by affidavit. An unsigned paper shall be stricken unless omission of the signature is corrected promptly after being called to the attention of the attorney or party.” (Code Civ. Proc., 128.7, subd. (a).) Plaintiff’s complaint was unsigned. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 7; Exhs. A-B.) Lockett brought to Plaintiff’s attention that service was unperfected and defective, which Plaintiff did not correct. (Lockett Decl., ¶ 9; Exh. C.) Therefore, pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 128.7, subdivision (a), the unsigned papers shall be stricken. 

Additionally, Plaintiff does not oppose this motion or demonstrate correction of the unperfected and defective service. Thus, the Court finds that Whisonant is entitled to have default set aside.  

 

IV. CONCLUSION 

Defendant Whisonant’s motion to vacate entry of default is GRANTED. 

 

Moving Party is ordered to give notice. 

 

DATED: July 2, 2026

Hon. Alexander C.D. Giza 

Judge of the Superior Court

Case Number: 25STCV26501    Hearing Date: July 2, 2026    Dept: 730

TENTATIVE 

 

  1. The Complaint 

 

On September 10, 2025, Plaintiff Chelette Dewees (“Plaintiff”) filed a Complaint against Defendant Gen Restaurant Companies LLC (“Defendant”) and DOES 1 through 50, alleging causes of action for: (1) Unruh Civil Rights Act (Cal. Civ. Code §§51-53); (2) California Disabled Persons Act (Cal. Civ. Code § 54.1); (3) Premises Liability (Cal. Civ. Code § 1714(a)); and (4) Negligence. Specifically, the Complaint alleged that Defendant failed to design, construct, maintain, and operate its website in compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (“ADA”) and California Unruh Civil Rights Act. (Compl., ¶¶5-7, 16-18, 20.) Furthermore, on or about July 1, 2025, at 8:40 p.m., Plaintiff slipped and fell inside of Defendant’s premises due to wet and/or uneven flooring. (Id., ¶19.) 

 

  1. Default Judgment 

 

All unnamed Doe defendants have been dismissed. 

 

In support of the default judgment package, Plaintiff submits her own declaration. However, Plaintiff merely provide exhibits showing that she visited Defendant’s restaurant premises on July 1, 2025; took a Lyft to Valley Medical Hospital; and a letter from her physician clearing her to return to physical activity. (Dewees Decl., ¶¶2-4, Exs. 1-4.) Contrarily, none of these documents show that Plaintiff incurred $2,500.00 in medical expenses; $2,500.00 in future medical expenses; and incurred $1,500.00 in Lyft rides to the hospital. Specifically, Plaintiff has not submitted any medical bills, letters from her physician that she will need future medical treatments and the cost of said treatment, and/or receipts or bank statements showing the amount she has paid for Lyft rides. Likewise, Plaintiff seeks $70,000.00 in general damages, which are largely disproportionate to claimed special damages of $6,500.00.  

 

To the extent Plaintiff claims she incurred $2,500.00 medical expenses, $1,500.00 in out of pocket travel expense via Lyft rides to the hospital, and anticipates expending $2,500.00 in future medical expenses, Plaintiff must submit evidence substantiating these claims. Furthermore, the Court will only award three times the amount in special damages proven for general damages.  

 

  1. Conclusion 

 

Based on the foregoing, Plaintiff Chelette Dewees’ request for default judgment submitted on May 12, 2026 is DENIED without prejudice. 

 

Case Number: 25STCV37140    Hearing Date: July 2, 2026    Dept: 730

Superior Court of California

County of Los Angeles

Department 730

 

NEDRA DIONE SHANNON,

Plaintiff,

vs.

MARIAN ARCENEAUX; BROWN & OWENS FAMILY LP,

Defendant(s).

Case No.:

25STCV37140

Hearing Date:

July 6, 2026

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: DEFENDANTS’ DEMURRER TO COMPLAINT AND MOTION TO STRIKE PORTIONS OF COMPLAINT

 

I.         BACKGROUND

Plaintiff Nedra Dione Shannon (“Plaintiff”) is an individual who rented and resided at 4206 Creed Ave, Los Angeles, California 90008 (the “Property”), a unit subject to the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance and the Anti-Tenant Harassment Ordinance. (Compl., ¶ 1.) Defendant Marian Arceneaux served as the manager and managing agent for the Property. (Id. at ¶ 2.) Defendant Brown & Owens Family LP is a California domestic partnership that owns and operates the Property. (Id. at ¶ 3.) The Property is a multi-unit residential rental property. (Id. at ¶ 5.)

On December 18, 2025, Plaintiff filed a Complaint against Defendants alleging twelve causes of action including (1) Violation of Los Angeles Anti-Tenant Harassment Ordinance (LAMC § 45.30 et seq.); (2) Retaliation (Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5); (3) Landlord Harassment/Illegal Conduct (Cal. Civ. Code § 1940.2); (4) Wrongful Entry/Violation of Right-of-Entry Statute  (Cal. Civ. Code § 1954); (5) Breach of Covenant of Quiet Enjoyment (Cal. Civ. Code § 1927); (6) Breach of the Implied Warranty of Habitability (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1941.1, 1941.3; H&S Code § 7920.3); (7) Negligent Per Se; (8) Private Nuisance; (9) Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress; (10) Invasion of Privacy; (11) Unfair Competition (Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200); and (12) Battery (Cal. Civ. Code § 1708).

The Complaint alleges a landlord-tenant dispute spanning five years. Plaintiff alleges that at move-in in August 2020 Defendants permitted potted plants and items in the rear common area. (Compl., ¶ 6.) In November 2020, during COVID, Defendants posted three notices threatening eviction over street-placed storage. (Ibid.) From November 2020 through August 2025, Plaintiff alleges that Defendants engaged in a continuing pattern of harassment and interference, including unlawful attempts and entries without notice, hostile and unannounced contacts at unreasonable hours, failure and delay in repair of defects, interference with access and parking, refusal to provide rent receipts, use of the Los Angeles Housing Department, and use of Public Health and inspections and city notices to demand or claim denied access and retaliate. (Id. at ¶ 7.)

On March 3, 2026, Defendants filed a Declaration of Demurring or Moving Party in Support of Automatic Extension because Defendants were unable to meet and confer with Plaintiff.

On March 4, 2026, Defendants filed this Demurrer and Motion to Strike. On June 25, 2026, Defendants filed a Reply and Notice of Non-Opposition. On June 30, 2026, Plaintiff filed a late opposition to the Demurrer and Motion to Strike.

 

II.        MEET AND CONFER REQUIREMENT

Before filing a demurrer pursuant to this chapter, the demurring party shall meet and confer in person, by telephone, or by video conference with the party who filed the pleading that is subject to demurrer for the purpose of determining whether an agreement can be reached that would resolve the objections to be raised in the demurrer. If an amended complaint, cross-complaint, or answer is filed, the responding party shall meet and confer again with the party who filed the amended pleading before filing a demurrer to the amended pleading. (Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 430.41, subd. (a).) A determination by the court that the meet and confer process was insufficient shall not be grounds to overrule or sustain a demurrer. (Id. at subd. (a)(4).) Civil Procedure section 435.5 similarly requires parties to meet and confer prior to a Motion to Strike and states that an insufficient meet and confer is not the grounds to grant or deny the motion. (Civ. Proc. Code § 435.5.)

Here, Defendants attempted to meet and confer with Plaintiffs prior to the filing of this demurrer and motion. (Diggs Decl., ¶ 3-12.) However, Defendants did not meet and confer with Plaintiffs prior to the filing of this demurrer and motion. (Id. at ¶ 12.) Although the meet and confer requirement was not met, the court will still analyze this Motion on its merits.

 

III.      LEGAL STANDARD on demurrer

As a general matter, in a demurrer proceeding, the defects must be apparent on the face of the pleading or via proper judicial notice. (Donabedian v. Mercury Ins. Co. (2004) 116 Cal.App.4th 968, 994.) “A demurrer tests the pleading alone, and not the evidence or facts alleged.” (E-Fab, Inc. v. Accountants, Inc. Servs. (2007) 153 Cal.App.4th 1308, 1315.) As such, the court assumes the truth of the complaint’s properly pleaded or implied factual allegations. (Ibid.) The only issue a demurrer is concerned with is whether the complaint, as it stands, states a cause of action. (Hahn v. Mirda (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 747.)

 “The party against whom a complaint or cross-complaint has been filed may object, by demurrer or answer as provided in section 430.30, to the pleading on any one or more of the following grounds... (e) the pleading does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. (f) The pleading is uncertain. As used in this subdivision, “uncertain” includes ambiguous and unintelligible." (Code Civ. Proc., § 430.10.) “[D]emurrers for uncertainty are disfavored, and are granted only if the pleading is so incomprehensible that a defendant cannot reasonably respond.” (A.J. Fistes Corp. v. GDL Best Contractors, Inc. (2019) 38 Cal.App.5th 677, 695.)

Where a demurrer is sustained, leave to amend must be allowed where there is a reasonable possibility of successful amendment. (Goodman v. Kennedy (1976) 18 Cal.3d 335, 348.) The burden is on the plaintiff to show the court that a pleading can be amended successfully. (Id. [AW15.1]; Lewis v. YouTube, LLC (2015) 244 Cal.App.4th 118, 226.) However, “[i]f there is any reasonable possibility that the plaintiff can state a good cause of action, it is error to sustain a demurrer without leave to amend.” (Youngman v. Nevada Irrigation Dist. (1969) 70 Cal.2d 240, 245).

           

IV.       DISCUSSION

A.    SEVENTH CAUSE OF ACTION FOR NEGLIGENCE PER SE

Defendants argue Plaintiff’s seventh cause of action fails because Plaintiff did not add any independent factual or legal basis for relief. Rather, Plaintiff merely restates the same statutory violations of Civil Code §§ 1954, 1940.2, 1942.5, 1927, 1941.1, 1941.3, Health & Safety Code § 17920.3, and LAMC § 45.30 et seq. stated in the First through Sixth Causes of Action as a separate negligence per se cause of action. Additionally, Negligence Per Se is not a separate cause of action.

In opposition, Plaintiff acknowledges the Evidence Code section 669 operates as an evidentiary doctrine creating a presumption of negligence based on statutory violations. Plaintiff argues that the allegations supporting negligence per se are still relevant.

The court finds Plaintiff’s arguments unpersuasive. “[T]he doctrine of negligence per se is not a separate cause of action, but creates an evidentiary presumption that affects the standard of care in a cause of action for negligence.” (Goldstein v. Superior Ct. (2023) 93 Cal.App.5th 736, 741.)

Because the doctrine of negligence per se is not a separate cause of action and Plaintiff has already stated direct causes of action under Civil Code §§ 1954, 1940.2, 1942.5, 1927, 1941.1, 1941.3, Health & Safety Code § 17920.3, and LAMC § 45.30 et seq., the cause of action for negligence per se is merely duplicative. A demurrer may be sustained when a cause of action is duplicative of another cause of action and “thus adds nothing to the complaint by way of fact or theory of recovery.” (Rodrigues v. Campbell Industries (1978) 87 Cal.App.3d 494, 501; see Palm Springs Villas II Homeowners Association, Inc. v. Parth (2016) 248 Cal.App.4th 268, 290.) Plaintiff has failed to provide additional, independent factual basis for the negligence per se cause of action.

Accordingly, the demurrer to the seventh cause of action is sustained without leave to amend.

 

B.    NINTH cause of action for intentional infliction of emotional distress

To state a claim for intentional infliction of emotional distress (“IIED”), a plaintiff must allege: (1) extreme and outrageous conduct by the defendant; (2) intention to cause, or reckless disregard of the probability of causing, emotional distress; (3) severe emotional distress; and (4) actual and proximate causation. (Hughes v. Pair (2009) 46 Cal.4th 1035, 1050) The conduct must be "so extreme as to exceed all bounds of that usually tolerated in a civilized community." (Id. at 1051.) Liability for IIED does not extend to mere insults, indignities, threats, annoyances, petty oppressions, or other trivialities. (Crouch v. Trinity Christian Ctr. of Santa Ana, Inc. (2019) 39 Cal. App. 5th 995, 1007.)

 

Defendants argue that the Ninth Cause of Action characterizes conduct ordinary landlord-tenant interactions as “extreme and outrageous.” Because the ninth cause of action fails to allege conduct rising to the “extreme and outrageous” standard, it must be dismissed.

 

In opposition, Plaintiff contends the Complaint alleges conduct that goes beyond ordinary landlord-tenant disputes. Plaintiff argues that whether the conduct was sufficiently extreme and outrageous is a fact-intensive question that should not be resolved against Plaintiff at the pleading stage. Moreover, the Complaint alleges a prolonged course of conduct affecting Plaintiff’s home, safety, privacy, and housing security.

 

Here, Plaintiff’s ninth cause of action alleges:

 

“Such conduct was not mere indignities or annoyances, but included: repeated unlawful and pretextual entries (including the locksmith entry of May 2, 2025); public multi-page postings taped to Plaintiff’s doors and windows and a bright yellow packet deliberately obscuring her security camera; covering her camera outright; late-night and early-morning calls and voicemails (including around 3:00 a.m.); bringing police and a filming crew to Plaintiff’s home absent any emergency; physically aggressive contact when Defendant shoved a door into Plaintiff in February 2024; a June 2024 doorway tussle causing Plaintiff physical injury to her hand; and serial unlawful detainer filings (3/27/24; 11/26/24; 8/27/25) initiated to intimidate and pressure Plaintiff to vacate.”

 

(Compl., ¶ 125.)

 

 

Assuming these facts to be true, Plaintiff has sufficiently pleaded facts to demonstrate that that Defendants’ conduct was “extreme and outrageous.” Plaintiff sufficiently pleaded facts such as middle-of-the-night calls, physical contact such as shoving doors, calling the police without emergency, and filing multiple unlawful detainers that may constitute extreme and outrageous behavior.

 

Moreover, Defendants rely on Newby v. Alto Riviera Apartments (1976) 60 Cal.App.3d 288, 297-98 to argue that courts have rejected IIED claims based on more aggressive behavior than alleged here. This reliance is misplaced. There, the Court found the appellant presented substantial evidence that the respondents’ behavior was outrageous. (Newby v. Alto Riviera Apartments (1976) 60 Cal.App.3d 288, 297-98.) There, the manager shouted at the appellant and ordered her out of the apartment in three days. (Ibid.) Here, Plaintiff alleges to have dealt with aggressive behavior and multiple unlawful detainer filings. Thus, Plaintiff has sufficiently plead facts to demonstrate extreme or outrageous behavior.

 

Accordingly, the demurrer to the ninth cause of action is overruled.

           

 

C.    twelfth cause of action for battery

The elements of a civil battery are: (1) defendant intentionally did an act which resulted in a harmful or offensive contact with the plaintiff's person, (2) plaintiff did not consent to the contact, and (3) the harmful or offensive contact caused injury, damage, loss, or harm to the plaintiff. (Piedra v. Dugan (2004) 123 Cal.App.4th 1483, 1495.)

 

            Defendants argue that the twelfth cause of action is fatally vague and conclusory. The Complaint fails to allege the context in which the alleged dispute on February 16 occurred, whether it was during a disputed entry, who initiated the contact, whether Defendant Arceneaux touched Plaintiff, and whether an actual injury resulted. Additionally, the June 2024 allegation is deficient because it does not identify the date, location, or circumstances of the incident.

 

            In opposition, Plaintiff argues the allegations were sufficient to plead battery because they allege intentional conduct resulting in harmful or offensive contact without consent. Additionally, Plaintiff contends Defendants’ argument that more detail is needed concerns evidentiary matters better addressed in discovery.

 

            The twelfth cause of action alleges:

           

“On or about February 16, 2024, Defendant [Arceneaux], acting individually and as managing agent for Owner Defendant, intentionally and without consent snatched a door from Plaintiff’s grasp and forcefully pushed it into Plaintiff’s back while Plaintiff was standing on the porch. The contact was offensive, unconsented to, and caused Plaintiff pain, fear, and humiliation in the presence of her children.

 

On or about June 2024, during a purported “emergency” entry, Defendant escalated a confrontation at the doorway, resulting in a physical tussle in which Plaintiff’s hand was injured, requiring medical attention. The contact was intentional, unprivileged, and caused Plaintiff physical harm.”

 

(Compl., ¶ 147-148.)

 

Assuming these facts to be true, Plaintiff has sufficiently pled facts to demonstrate Defendant Arceneaux’s intentional act (such as snatching the door, forcefully pushing it, and escalating the confrontation) resulted in harmful or offensive conduct (such as humiliation, fear, pain, and necessitating medical attention) and that the plaintiff did not consent to that conduct. The Court does not agree with the Defendants’ assertion that additional context is necessary to meet the level of specificity to state a claim for civil battery.

 

Accordingly, the demurrer to the twelfth cause of action is overruled.

 

 

D.    uncertainty

A demurrer for uncertainty lies when a complaint is "ambiguous or unintelligible." (Code Civ. Proc. § 430.10(f).) “A demurrer for uncertainty is strictly construed, even where a complaint is in some respects uncertain, because ambiguities can be clarified under modern discovery procedures.” (Khoury v. Maly’s of California, Inc. (1993) 14 Cal.App.4th 612, 616.) “The objection of uncertainty does not go to the failure to allege sufficient facts.” (Brea v. McGlashan (1934) 3 Cal.App.2d 454, 459.) “It goes to the doubt as to what the pleader means by the facts alleged.” (Id.) “Such a demurrer should not be sustained where the allegations of the complaint are sufficiently clear to apprise the defendant of the issues which he is to meet.” (People v. Lim (1941) 18 Cal.2d 872, 882.)

 

      Defendants contends that the Complaint is uncertain because (1) it pleads 73 paragraphs of background; (2) its prayer for relief is overlapping and duplicative; and (3) it fails to specify the dates of the acts which establish a “continuing pattern” of conduct.

     

      In opposition, Plaintiff argues that Defendants may disagree as to the detail of the Complaint, but Defendants cannot reasonably claim to be unable to understand the claims. Moreover, additional factual detail can be obtained through discovery.

 

The Court agrees with Plaintiff. The Court does not find Defendant’s arguments to be persuasive. The Complaint is not so uncertain to make it unintelligible.

 

 

E.    LITIGATION PRIVILEGE

 

Defendants argue that the Litigation Privilege bars the first, second, third, and eleventh causes of action because they were based on filing unlawful detainer actions.

 

In opposition, Plaintiff argues the Litigation Privilege does not bar these causes of action. The unlawful detainer actions included in the Complaint are alleged as part of the factual chronology and context of Defendants’ course of conduct. Plaintiff argues the Litigation Privilege does not eliminate claims based on separate wrongful conduct merely because litigation-related events are referenced to in the Complaint.

 

To sustain a demurrer upon an affirmative defense, the affirmative defense must clearly appear on the face of the complaint. (See CrossTalk Productions, Inc. v. Jacobson (1998) 65 Cal.App.4th 631, 635.) “A demurrer based on an affirmative defense cannot properly be sustained where the action might be barred by the defense, but is not necessarily barred.” (Ibid.)

 

A privileged publication or broadcast is one made: In any (1) legislative proceeding, (2) judicial proceeding, (3) in any other official proceeding authorized by law, or (4) in the initiation or course of any other proceeding authorized by law and reviewable pursuant to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 1084) of Title 1 of Part 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (Civ. Code § 47, subd. (b).) The usual formulation is that the privilege applies to any communication (1) made in judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings; (2) by litigants or other participants authorized by law; (3) to achieve the objects of the litigation; and (4) that have some connection or logical relation to the action. (Silberg v. Anderson (1990) 50 Cal.3d 205, 212.)

 

A threshold issue in determining if the litigation privilege applies is whether the alleged injury arises from a communicative act or noncommunicative conduct. (Action Apartment Assn., Inc. v. City of Santa Monica (2007) 41 Cal. 4th 1232, 1248.) The key in determining whether the privilege applies is whether the injury allegedly resulted from an act that was communicative in its essential nature. (Ibid.) For example, the following acts have been deemed communicative and thus protected by the litigation privilege: attorney prelitigation solicitations of potential clients and subsequent filing of pleadings in the litigation, and testimonial use of the contents of illegally overheard conversation. The following acts have been deemed noncommunicative and thus unprivileged: prelitigation illegal recording of confidential telephone conversations; eavesdropping on a telephone conversation; and physician's negligent examination of patient causing physical injury. (Ibid.) The court draws “a careful distinction between a cause of action based squarely on a privileged communication, such as an action for defamation, and one based upon an underlying course of conduct evidenced by the communication. (Ibid.) “As a general rule, the privilege ‘ “applies only to communicative acts and does not privilege tortious courses of conduct.” ’ (Id. at p. 1249.) The filing of a legal action is not “an independent, noncommunicative, wrongful act.” (Id.)

 

Here, the affirmative defense does not clearly bar the causes of action. There are no protected communications from unlawful detainer actions included in or attached to the Complaint. Moreover, while legal filings are communicative actions, the Complaint uses the legal filings to allege that Plaintiff was harassed and pressured to vacate by the Defendants. (See Compl., ¶ 77.) The filing of unlawful detainer actions is listed as one of multiple allegedly harassing actions conducted by Defendants. (Ibid.) Thus, because the Litigation Privilege applies only to communicative acts, not tortious conducts, and must clearly bar the cause of action, the Litigation Privilege is not applicable.

 

Accordingly, the demurrer to first, second, third, and eleventh causes of action are overruled.

 

F.     CAUSES OF ACTION AGAINST DEFENDANT MARIAN ARCENEAUX

 

i.       Defendant Arceneaux is Alleged to be a Property Manager

 

Defendants argue that the Complaint must be dismissed as to Defendant Arceneaux (“Arceneaux”) because the allegations establish she acted exclusively in her capacity as Managing General Partner of Brown & Owens LP, not as an individual. Defendants further argue that as a general partner acting within her authority, Arceneaux is not liable for the entity’s obligations. Because Arceneaux’s actions were within the scope of a managing general partner’s authority, Defendant Brown & Owens Family LP is legally responsible, not Arceneaux, for causes of action one through eight, ten, and eleven.

 

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that Defendants’ contention that Arceneaux cannot be individually liable because she acted only in a representative capacity is premature. Plaintiff argues that a person who personally participates in tortious conduct is not automatically shielded from liability merely because she also acted as an agent or manager.

 

Here, the Complaint states that Arceneaux “is an individual who, at all relevant times, served as the manager and managing agent for the Subject Property on behalf of the owning limited partnership, with authority over access, repairs, inspections, notices, and rent-related communications affecting Plaintiff’s tenancy.” (Compl., ¶ 2.) These allegations establish that Arceneaux is a “manager and managing agent” for the Property, rather than the manager of the Limited Partnership. Thus, Defendants have not established that the Complaint alleges that Arceneaux is a managing agent of the limited partnership.

 

Accordingly, Defendants’ demurrer to the Complaint because Arceneaux is a general partner is overruled.

 

ii. Statutory Causes of Action and Allegations of Individual Liability

 

Defendants argue that the statutory causes of actions under LAMC § 45.32, Civil Code § 1942.5 (retaliation), Civil Code § 1940.2 (harassment), Civil Code § 1954 (wrongful entry), and Civil Code § 1927 (quiet enjoyment) all impose obligations on the “owner” or the “landlord” of the premises, not an individual who manages the property in representative capacity. Because Defendant Brown & Owens Family LP is the owner and landlord it is the proper defendant for these statutory claims, not Arceneaux.

 

First, the first cause of action under LAMC § 45.32 defines a “landlord” as referring to “any owner, lessor, sublessor, manager, and/or person, including any firm, corporation, partnership, or other entity, having any legal or equitable right of ownership or possession or the right to lease or receive rent for the use and occupancy of a rental unit, and whether acting as principal or through an agent or representative or successor of any of the foregoing.” (LAMC § 45.32.) This definition of “landlord” includes a “manager.” The Complaint has sufficiently plead that Arceneaux is a manager of the Property. Thus, the first cause of action cannot be sustained on these grounds.

 

Similarly, the fifth cause of action under Civil Code § 1927 does not specifically state it must be brought against a landlord. The section states: “An agreement to let upon hire binds the letter to secure to the hirer the quiet possession of the thing hired during the term of the hiring, against all persons lawfully claiming the same.” (Civ. Code § 1927.) Thus, the fifth cause of action cannot be sustained on these grounds.

 

Next, the second cause of action under Civil Code § 1942.5, the third cause of action under Civil Code § 1940.2, and the fourth cause of action under Civil Code § 1954 all require liability from a landlord, which does not specifically include a property manager. The Complaint does not plead that Arceneaux is a landlord. Instead, it states that owner and operator of the Property is Defendant Brown & Ownes Family LP. Thus, the demurrer to the second, third, and fourth causes of action is sustained.

 

Furthermore, in the second, third, and fourth causes of action are not sufficiently plead. To sufficiently plead claims under statutes that require landlord liability, Plaintiff would either need to plead that Arceneaux was a landlord or that Arceneaux was the alter ego of the limited partnership. Here, the Complaint does neither.

 

Accordingly, the demurrer to second, third, and fourth causes of action is sustained with leave to amend. The demurrer to the first and fifth causes of action against the Arceneaux is overruled.

 

           

V.        LEGAL sTANDARD ON MOTION TO sTRIKE

The court may, upon a motion, or at any time in its discretion, and upon terms it deems proper, strike any irrelevant, false, or improper matter inserted in any pleading. (Code Civ. Proc., § 436(a).) The court may also strike all or any part of any pleading not drawn or filed in conformity with the laws of this state, a court rule, or an order of the court. (Id., § 436(b).) The grounds for a motion to strike are that the pleading has irrelevant, false or improper matter, or has not been drawn or filed in conformity with laws. (Id., § 436.) The grounds for moving to strike must appear on the face of the pleading or by way of judicial notice. (Id., § 437.)

 

vI.       DISCUSSION

            A. PUNITIVE DAMAGES

Defendants argue that punitive damages allegations must be stricken as to (1) Defendant Brown & Ownes Family LP because no corporate ratification was alleged and (2) Defendant Arceneaux because no individual liability was alleged.

 

In opposition, Plaintiff contends that Plaintiff alleges willful, malicious, oppressive, and bad-faith conduct sufficient to support punitive damages allegations at the pleading stage. Plaintiff argues that the Complaint alleges that Arceneaux served as manager and managing agent for the Property, which was sufficient at the pleading stage.

 

According to Civil Procedure section 3294(b):

 

“An employer shall not be liable for damages pursuant to subdivision (a), based upon acts of an employee of the employer, unless the employer had advance knowledge of the unfitness of the employee and employed him or her with a conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others or authorized or ratified the wrongful conduct for which the damages are awarded or was personally guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice. With respect to a corporate employer, the advance knowledge and conscious disregard, authorization, ratification or act of oppression, fraud, or malice must be on the part of an officer, director, or managing agent of the corporation.”

 

When the defendant is a corporation, “the oppression, fraud, or malice must be perpetrated, authorized, or knowingly ratified by an officer, director, or managing agent of the corporation.” (Wilson v. Southern California Edison Company (2015) 234 Cal.App.4th 123, 164; see Civ. Code § 3294(b).) Civil Code section 3294 authorizes the recovery of punitive damages in non-contract cases where “the defendant has been guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice . . . .” (Civ. Code § 3294(a).) “‘Malice’ means conduct which is intended by the defendant to cause injury to the plaintiff or despicable conduct which is carried on by the defendant with a willful and conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others.” (Id., § 3294(c)(1).) A plaintiff must establish the defendant was aware of the probable dangerous consequences of his conduct and that he willfully and deliberately failed to avoid those consequences to support an award of punitive damages based on conscious disregard of the safety of others. (Penner v. Falk (1984) 153 Cal.App.3d 858, 867.) “‘Oppression’ means despicable conduct that subjects a person to cruel and unjust hardship in conscious disregard of that person’s rights.” (Civ. Code § 3294(c)(2).) “‘Fraud’ means an intentional misrepresentation, deceit, or concealment of a material fact known to the defendant with the intention on the part of the defendant of thereby depriving a person of property or legal rights or otherwise causing injury.” (Id., § 3294(c)(3).)

 

Punitive damages thus require more than the mere commission of a tort. (See Taylor v. Superior Court (1979) 24 Cal.3d 890, 894-95.) Specific facts must be pleaded in support of punitive damages. (See Hillard v. A.H. Robins Co. (1983) 148 Cal.App.3d 374, 391-92.)

 

Here, Plaintiff seeks punitive damages on the second, third, fourth, seventh, ninth, tenth, and twelfth causes of action. (See Compl.) Because the demurrer to the seventh cause of action was sustained, the issue as to the seventh cause of action is moot as to both Defendants. Additionally, the issue is moot as to the second, third, and fourth causes of action for Defendant Arceneaux.

 

The Court agrees with Defendants that the Complaint contains no allegations identifying any officer, director, partner, or managing agent of the limited partnership who authorized, ratified, or engaged in alleged oppressive conduct on behalf of the entity. Arceneaux is alleged to be a manager of the property, not a managing general partner. (Compl., ¶ 2.) Thus, the motion to strike punitive damages against Defendant Brown & Owens Family LP is granted with leave to amend.

 

As for Defendant Arceneaux, the Court must consider whether punitive damages were sufficiently plead as for the non-moot causes of action, which are the ninth, tenth, and twelfth causes of action. The Complaint is sufficiently plead as to each of these causes of action. Each cause of action alleges conduct intended by Arceneaux to cause injury to the Plaintiff or despicable conduct which is carried on by Arceneaux with a willful and conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others. (Civ. Code § 3294(c)(1).) The ninth cause of action for IIED alleges conduct such as late night calls, bringing police and a filming crew to Plaintiff’s home absent emergency, physically aggressive conduct, and serial unlawful detainer filings intended to intimidate and pressure Plaintiff to vacate and which caused Plaintiff anxiety, humiliation, fear, sleep disturbance, and mental anguish. (Compl., ¶ 125, 127.) The tenth cause of action for invasion of privacy alleges conduct such as a locksmith entering without notice, obstructing Plaintiff’s security camera, surveilling Plaintiff’s doors, and filming Plaintiff. The twelfth cause of action pleads allegations that on two different occasions Arceneaux physically harmed or injured Plaintiff. Thus, Plaintiff sufficiently plead allegations that Arceneaux intended to cause injury or was despicable conduct in disregard of the rights or safety of Plaintiff. Accordingly, the request to strike punitive damages against Arceneaux for the non-moot ninth, tenth, and twelfth causes of action is denied.

 

 

            b.  DUPLICATIVE, uNCERTAIN, OR LACKS SPECIFICITY

Defendants argue that (1) treble damages must be stricken as duplicative and uncertain; (2) requests for civil penalties “per violation” must be stricken for lack of factual specificity; (3) paragraph 148 in the complaint must be stricken as vague and uncertain; (4) all statutory damages under Penal Code § 637.2 must be stricken as premature and speculative; and (5) the prayer for relief must be stricken due to duplicative damages.

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that (1) the request for treble damages is not duplicative; (2) that the civil penalty allegations are sufficiently specific; (3) paragraph 148 is sufficiently specific; (4) damages under Penal Code § 637.2 should not be stricken as specific dates and recordings are not yet known and will likely be found during discovery; (5) Defendants’ concern about overlapping damages is premature.

The Court finds Defendants’ arguments unpersuasive and improper for a Motion to Strike. The standard for a motion to strike is not whether the pleading is duplicative, uncertain, or lacks specificity, as suggested by Defendants. Instead, the court may strike any irrelevant, false, or improper matter inserted in the pleading. (Code Civ. Proc., § 436(a).) Defendants’ contentions have not properly met the standard for a motion to strike. For this reason, Defendants’ arguments are unpersuasive and the motion to strike is denied.

 

VII.     CONCLUSION

Based on the foregoing, Plaintiff’s Demurrer is sustained in part and overruled in part and Plaintiff’s Motion to Strike is granted in part and denied in part.

The demurrer to the seventh cause of action is sustained without leave to amend as to both Defendants. The demurrer to the ninth and twelfth causes of action is overruled. The demurrer to the second, third, and fourth causes of action as to Defendant Marian Arceneaux is sustained with leave to amend. The demurrer to the first and fifth causes of action as to Defendant Marian Arceneaux is overruled.

The Motion to Strike punitive damages against Defendant Brown & Owens Family LP is granted with leave to amend. The remainder of the Motion to Strike is denied.

Moving Party is ordered to give notice.

Case Number: 25STCV38426    Hearing Date: July 2, 2026    Dept: 730

Superior Court of California

County of Los Angeles

Department 730

 

ERICK GARCIA MIRELES,

Plaintiff(s),

vs.

GENERAL MOTORS LLC, et al.,

Defendant(s).

Case No.:

25STCV38426

Hearing Date:

July 6, 2026

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR ATTORNEY’S FEES, COSTS, AND EXPENSES

 

I.         BACKGROUND

On December 31, 2025, Plaintiff Erick Garcia Mireles (“Plaintiff”) filed a Complaint against Defendants General Motors LLC and Does 1 through 10, inclusive (“Defendants”) alleging causes of action for (1) Breach of Implied Warranty of Merchantability Cal. Civ. Code §1794; (2) Breach of Implied Warranty of Fitness Cal. Civ. Code §1794; (3) Breach of Express Warranty Cal. Civ. Code §1794; (4) Failure to Promptly Repurchase Product Cal. Civ. Code §1793.2(d); (5) Failure to Commence Repairs within a Reasonable Time and to Complete them Within 30 Days Cal. Civ. Code §1794; and (6) Violation of Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act. On May 27, 2026, Notice of Settlement of Entire Case was filed.

On June 4, 2026, Plaintiff filed this Motion for Attorney’s Fees, Costs, and Expenses. On June 11, 2026, Plaintiff filed an Amended Motion for Attorney’s Fees, Costs, and Expenses (“Motion”). On June 22, 2026, Defendant filed an opposition. On June 25, 2026, Plaintiff filed a reply.

 

II.        LEGAL STANDARD

            Attorneys’ fees are allowed as costs when authorized by contract, statute, or law. (Code Civ. Proc, § 1033.5, subd. (a)(10)(B).) In a lemon law action, costs and expenses, including attorney’s fees, may be recovered by a prevailing buyer under the Song-Beverly Act. (See Civ. Code, § 1794(d).) 

Civil Code section 1794[1] provides: “If the buyer prevails in an action under this section, the buyer shall be allowed by the court to recover as part of the judgment a sum equal to the aggregate amount of costs and expenses, including attorney’s fees based on actual time expended, determined by the court to have been reasonably incurred by the buyer in connection with the commencement and prosecution of such action.” (§ 1794.) 

Thus, the statute includes a “reasonable attorney’s fees” standard.  The attorney bears the burden of proof as to “reasonableness” of any fee claim. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1033.5(c)(5).) This burden requires competent evidence as to the nature and value of the services rendered. (Martino v. Denevi (1986) 182 Cal.App.3d 553, 559.) “Testimony of an attorney as to the number of hours worked on a particular case is sufficient evidence to support an award of attorney fees, even in the absence of detailed time records.” (Ibid.) 

A plaintiff’s verified billing invoices are prima facie evidence that the costs, expenses, and services listed were necessarily incurred. (See Hadley v. Krepel (1985) 167 Cal.App.3d 677, 682.) “In challenging attorney fees as excessive because too many hours of work are claimed, it is the burden of the challenging party to point to the specific items challenged, with a sufficient argument and citations to the evidence. General arguments that fees claimed are excessive, duplicative, or unrelated do not suffice.” (Lunada Biomedical v. Nunez (2014) 230 Cal.App.4th 459, 488, quoting Premier Med. Mgmt. Sys., Inc. v. California Ins. Guarantee Ass’n (2008) 163 Cal.App.4th 550, 564.) The Court has discretion to reduce fees that result from inefficient or duplicative use of time. (Horsford v. Bd. of Trustees of California State Univ. (2005) 132 Cal. App. 4th 359, 395.) 

In determining a reasonable attorney fee, the trial court begins with the lodestar, i.e., the number of hours reasonably expended multiplied by the reasonable hourly rate. (Warren v. Kia Motors America, Inc. (2018) 30 Cal.App.5th 24, 36.) The lodestar may then be adjusted based on factors specific to the case in order to fix the fee at the fair market value of the legal services provided. (Ibid.) These facts include (1) the novelty and difficulty of the questions involved, (2) the skill displayed in presenting them, (3) the extent to which the nature of the litigation precluded other employment by the attorneys, (4) the contingent nature of the fee award. (Ibid.) 

 

III.      DISCUSSION

Plaintiffs move for an award of attorney fees and costs in the total amount of $29,013.30, consisting of (1) $18,566 in attorney’s fees, (2) a lodestar enhancement of 1.5 in the amount of $9,416.50 for attorney’s fees of $27,982.50, and (3) $1,030.80 in costs and expenses.

 

A.    Entitlement to Attorney’s Fees

It is undisputed that Plaintiff is the prevailing party in this action, and is therefore entitled to attorney fees, costs, and expenses pursuant to section 1794(d).

 

B.    Reasonableness of Fees

a.      Reasonable Hourly Rate

“The reasonable hourly rate is that prevailing in the community for similar work.” (PLCM Group v. Drexler (2000) 22 Cal.4th 1084, 1095.) “The experienced trial judge is the best judge of the value of professional services rendered in [her] court.” (Ibid.)

Plaintiff seeks to recover attorney’s fees for attorney Atam Rostomyan (“Rostomyan”). Rostomyan’s rate is $650 per hour. (Rostomyan Decl., ¶ 17.) Rostomyan’s rate is reasonable given his experience, education, skill, and the prevailing market rates in Los Angeles County. (Id. at ¶ 17-24.) Rostomyan attests to being an attorney since 2014 (about 12 years of experience) with substantial litigation experience. (Id. at ¶ 18.) Rostomyan also attests to practicing at his own firm, Rostomyan Law, PC which focuses on Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act claims and employment actions. (Id. at ¶ 19.) Additionally, Rostomyan attests to successfully handling hundreds, if not thousands, of lemon law cases within the last 8 years. (Id. at ¶ 22.)

Defendants argue the hourly rate exceeds the market rate for lemon law actions, which is $350.00. Defendants seek to reduce Rostomyan’s rate to reflect the 2021 Real Rate Report. Defendants contend that the First Quartile rate for general liability in Los Angeles is $304 for partners and the First Quartile rate for firms with less than 50 attorneys or less is $200 for partners. Accordingly, the rates should be average for a reasonable rate of $252 for partners. (MAR Decl., ¶ 12.)

Based on this Court’s experience in approving legal rates for lemon law actions, Rostomyan’s rate of $650.00 per hour for around 12 years of experience as an attorney and 8 years of lemon law experience is on the high end. For example, the Court has previously approved rates of $650 for attorneys with twenty or more years of experience. The Court has approved rates ranging between $350.00 to $385.00 for attorneys with over five years of experience in lemon law. Thus, the Court finds Rostomyan has not justified the rate of $650.00 per hour and will therefore reduce the rate to $385.00 per hour.  

 

b.     Reasonable Hours Incurred

“A trial court assessing attorney fees begins with a touchstone or lodestar figure, based on the ‘careful compilation of the time spent and reasonable hourly compensation of each attorney ... involved in the presentation of the case.” (Christian Research Institute v. Alnor (2008) 165 Cal.App.4th 1315, 1321.) “The reasonableness of attorney fees is within the discretion of the trial court, to be determined from a consideration of such factors as the nature of the litigation, the complexity of the issues, the experience and expertise of counsel and the amount of time involved. The court may also consider whether the amount requested is based upon unnecessary or duplicative work.” (Wilkerson v. Sullivan (2002) 99 Cal.App.4th 443, 448.) A reduced award might be fully justified by a general observation that an attorney overlitigated a case or submitted a padded bill or that the opposing party has stated valid objections. (Gorman v. Tassajara Development Corp. (2009) 178 Cal.App.4th 44, 101.) 

A plaintiff’s verified billing invoices are prima facie evidence that the costs, expenses, and services listed were necessarily incurred. (See Hadley v. Krepel (1985) 167 Cal.App.3d 677, 682.) Plaintiff included his hourly billing with this Motion. (Rostomyan Decl., ¶ 7 [Exh. B].) Plaintiff seeks to recover attorney’s fees for 28.7 hours. (Ibid.) Rostomyan contends he did not bill for clerical tasks. (Id. at ¶ 10.)

In opposition, Defendants contend that fees such as scheduling mediation are administrative tasks that should not be billed for. Additionally, entries such as received and reviewed fully executed retainer agreement, informed the client regarding mediation date and mediation, received and reviewed the court’s minute order are routine tasks that should not be paid at a premium rate. Furthermore, Defendants contend that Lemon Law litigators rely on boilerplate templates and the use of block billing for preparation of pleadings should be reduced. Given Rostomyan’s experience, these tasks should not have taken as long.

 

 The Court finds no basis to strike these bills or reduce specific entries Defendants argue could have been billed at a lower rate, especially as the Court has already reduced the attorney billing rate. The Court does not find that the 15 minutes spent scheduling mediation with the mediator was an administrative task to be removed.

Accordingly, Plaintiff’s 28.7 hours is not reduced.

 

C.    Multiplier

While the lodestar reflects the basic fee for comparable legal services in the community, it may be adjusted based on various factors, including “(1) the novelty and difficulty of the questions involved, and the skill displayed in presenting them; (2) the extent to which the nature of the litigation precluded other employment by the attorneys; (3) the contingent nature of the fee award” and (4) the success achieved. (Serrano v. Priest (1977) 20 Cal.3d 25, 49.) 

Nonetheless, the court must not consider extraordinary skill and the other Serrano factors to the extent these are already included with the lodestar. (Ketchum v. Moses (2001) 24 Cal.4th 1122, 1138-1139.) “[A] trial court should award a multiplier for exceptional representation only when the quality of representation far exceeds the quality of representation that would have been provided by an attorney of comparable skill and experience billing at the hourly rate used in the lodestar calculation. Otherwise, the fee award will result in unfair double counting and be unreasonable.” (Id. at 1139.) 

Plaintiffs request a lodestar multiplier enhancement of 1.5. The Court finds that under the circumstances of this case, a lodestar multiplier is not appropriate. Nothing before the Court indicates that the case presented novel issues or that the quality of representation far exceeded the quality of representation that would have been provided by attorneys of comparable skill and experience billing at the same rates. Further, in terms of the contingency basis, the Court finds that such consideration and risk is already included within the lodestar amount. 

Accordingly, the Court declines to award a lodestar multiplier

 

D.    Costs

Allowable costs “shall be reasonably necessary to the conduct of the litigation rather than merely convenient or beneficial to its preparation.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 1033.5, subd. (c)(2).) Any items not specifically mentioned by statute “may be allowed or denied in the court's discretion.” (Id., subd. (c)(4).) The Beverly-Song Act allows a successful plaintiff to recover both “costs” and “expenses.” (§ 1794, subd. (d).)

“If the items appear to be proper charges the verified memorandum is prima facie evidence that the costs, expenses and services therein listed were necessarily incurred by the defendant [citations], and the burden of showing that an item is not properly chargeable or is unreasonable is upon the [objecting party].' [Citation.]” (Nelson v. Anderson (1999) 72 Cal.App.4th 111, 131.)¿

Plaintiff requests a total of $1,030.80 in costs and expenses. The cost items appear to be proper, and there was no opposition challenging any particular cost. Therefore, the Court awards Plaintiff the requested amount without any reductions. 

 

IV.       CONCLUSION

Based on the foregoing, Plaintiff’s motion for attorney’s fees is GRANTED IN PART. The Court awards Atam Rostomyan $11,049.50 in attorney’s fees and $1,030.80 in costs.

 

Moving Party is ordered to give notice.
